tags.label: Ideational
tags.definition: Populism as a thin-centred ideology, or set of ideas, that sets a pure people against a corrupt elite and wants politics to express the general will (Mudde, Hawkins).

tags.label: Discursive
tags.definition: Populism as a discourse or political logic that links unmet demands into ‘the people’ and sets it against those in power (Laclau, Mouffe, the Essex school).

tags.label: Political-strategic
tags.definition: Populism as a way of winning and using power, in which a personalistic leader relies on direct, unmediated support from a large and mostly unorganised following (Weyland).

tags.label: Performative or stylistic
tags.definition: Populism as a political style that is performed: appeals to ‘the people’ against ‘the elite’, ‘bad manners’, and the staging of crisis or threat (Moffitt).

tags.label: Socio-cultural
tags.definition: Populism as the flaunting of the ‘low’ in politics: manners, speech and tastes close to ordinary people, set against a ‘high’ that is polished and distant (Ostiguy).

tags.label: Economic or structural
tags.definition: Populism defined by economic policy or social structure: redistribution and spending that play down economic limits (Dornbusch and Edwards), or a cross-class coalition tied to a stage of development.

tags.label: Measurement and methods
tags.definition: Work on how to measure populism: attitude scales, text analysis of speeches and manifestos, expert surveys, and classifications of parties and leaders.

tags.label: Other or multiple
tags.definition: An approach not listed here, or a work that compares or combines three or more approaches, such as overviews, handbooks and conceptual debates.

tags.label: Foreign policy
tags.definition: What populists say and do in foreign policy: positions, decisions, diplomacy and relations with other states.

tags.label: Defence and security
tags.definition: Populism and defence or security policy: armed forces, military missions, defence spending, alliances, war and terrorism.

tags.label: The international sphere
tags.definition: Populism beyond the state: the EU and Euroscepticism, international organisations, multilateralism, the international order, and links between populists across borders.

tags.label: Parties, leaders and movements
tags.definition: The supply side: populist parties, leaders and movements themselves, their organisation, ideas and strategy, how they compete, and how other parties respond.

tags.label: Voters and attitudes
tags.definition: The demand side: who supports populists and why, including vote choice, populist attitudes and public opinion.

tags.label: Populists in government
tags.definition: What populists do in office, nationally or locally: how they govern, the policies they pass, and what changes as a result.

tags.label: Spatial populism
tags.definition: The geography of populism: urban–rural and centre–periphery divides, regions and places ‘left behind’, and local contexts of support.

tags.label: Economy and welfare
tags.definition: Economic causes and effects of populism: globalisation, trade, crisis and inequality, economic policy, and the welfare state, including welfare chauvinism.

tags.label: Media and communication
tags.definition: How populists communicate and how the media treat them: rhetoric, social media, news coverage and disinformation.

tags.label: Gender
tags.definition: Populism and gender: women and men as voters, members and leaders, masculinity and femininity, family policy and LGBTQ+ issues.

tags.label: Religion
tags.definition: Populism and religion: religious identity and language in populist politics, religious voters and organisations, and secularism.

tags.label: Migration
tags.definition: Populism and migration: immigration and asylum politics, nativism, borders, integration, and attitudes to migrants.

tags.label: Democracy and institutions
tags.definition: Populism and democracy: effects on liberal democracy, the rule of law, courts, parliaments and constitutions, democratic backsliding, and direct democracy.

tags.label: Other
tags.definition: A subject not listed here, such as climate, health or science. Recurring subjects become new tags, added to this file first.

region.label: Region
region.about: Where the populism studied takes place.

tags.label: Europe
tags.definition: The EU and the rest of Europe: the United Kingdom, the Western Balkans, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, Russia, Turkey and the South Caucasus.

tags.label: North America
tags.definition: The United States and Canada.

tags.label: Latin America
tags.definition: Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America.

tags.label: Asia-Pacific
tags.definition: Central, South, South-East and East Asia, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands.

tags.label: Middle East and North Africa
tags.definition: North Africa from Morocco to Egypt, and the Middle East from Israel and Palestine to the Gulf states, Yemen and Iran.

tags.label: Sub-Saharan Africa
tags.definition: Africa south of the Sahara, including Sudan and the Horn of Africa.

tags.label: Global or no regional focus
tags.definition: Works that cover three or more regions, or no region in particular, such as theory and concept work.

country.label: Country
country.about: The countries a work studies as cases.

method.label: Method
method.about: How the work studies its subject.

tags.label: Qualitative
tags.definition: Case studies, interviews, fieldwork, process tracing, archival work, and qualitative discourse or content analysis.

tags.label: Quantitative
tags.definition: Statistical analysis of numerical data such as election results, votes in parliament, expert surveys or economic indicators. Surveys, experiments and text-as-data have their own tags.

tags.label: Text-as-data (QTA)
tags.definition: Quantitative text analysis: dictionaries, scaling, topic models, machine learning and language models applied to speeches, manifestos, social media or news.

tags.label: Survey
tags.definition: Analysis of survey data on citizens or elites, including scales of populist attitudes.

tags.label: Experiment
tags.definition: Survey, conjoint, laboratory or field experiments.

tags.label: Mixed methods
tags.definition: Qualitative and quantitative methods combined in one design.

type.label: Type of publication
type.about: What kind of publication it is.

tags.label: Journal article
tags.definition: An article in an academic journal, including review articles.

tags.label: Book
tags.definition: A monograph, or an edited volume as a whole.

tags.label: Book chapter
tags.definition: A chapter in an edited volume or handbook.

tags.label: Policy paper
tags.definition: A report or brief from a think tank, an international organisation or a public body.

tags.label: Working paper
tags.definition: A working paper or preprint not yet published in a journal or book.

tags.label: Dataset
tags.definition: A published dataset, with its codebook.

oa.label: Open access
oa.about: Whether the work is free to read.

tags.label: Open access
tags.definition: The work is free to read, at the publisher or as a legal copy in a repository.

entries.title: Populism and International Relations: (Un)predictability, personalisation, and the reinforcement of existing trends in world politics
entries.abstract: As populists have formed governments all over the world, it becomes imperative to study the consequences of the rise of populism for International Relations. Yet, systematic academic analyses of the international impact of populist government formation are still missing, and political commentators tend to draw conclusions from few cases of right-wing populism in the Global North. But populism – conceptualised as a ‘thin’ ideology based on anti-elitism and anti-pluralism – takes different shapes across world regions as populists combine it with different ‘thick’ ideologies. To reflect such diversity and gain more systematic insights into the global implications of populism, we focus on cases of populist government formation in the Global South. We find that populists in power are not, per se, more belligerent or less willing to engage globally than their non-populist predecessors. Factors like status seeking or a country's embeddedness in international institutions mitigate the impact of populism. Its most immediate effect concerns procedural aspects: foreign policymaking becomes more centralised and personalised – yet, not entirely unpredictable, given the importance of ‘thick’ ideologies espoused by populist parties and leaders. Rather than changing course entirely, populists in power reinforce existing trends, especially a tendency towards diversifying international partnerships.
entries.citation: Destradi, Sandra, and Johannes Plagemann. 2019. “Populism and International Relations: (Un)Predictability, Personalisation, and the Reinforcement of Existing Trends in World Politics.” Review of International Studies 45 (5): 711–30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0260210519000184.

entries.title: Populism and the politicisation of foreign policy
entries.container: The British Journal of Politics and International Relations
entries.abstract: Populists in power often resort to the politicisation of foreign policy to generate domestic support. This article explores this process. First, it conceptualises populist politicisation of foreign policy. Second, it develops expectations on how such politicisation will take place: the distinctive features of populism (the intensity of populist discourse, the relative weight of anti-elitism and people-centrism, and a transnational understanding of the ‘people’ or the ‘elite’) will have an impact on how foreign policy is politicised. The empirical analysis focuses on selected public speeches and tweets by two populist leaders from the Global South: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Narendra Modi. The analysis reveals huge differences: the more populist Erdoğan emphasises anti-elitism and extensively resorts to the politicisation of Turkish foreign policy by constructing foreign threats. Modi is less populist and his discourse emphasises people-centrism; as expected, he only marginally politicises foreign policy, highlighting the greatness of the Indian nation.
entries.citation: Destradi, Sandra, Johannes Plagemann, and Hakkı Taş. 2022. “Populism and the Politicisation of Foreign Policy.” The British Journal of Politics and International Relations 24 (3): 475–92. https://doi.org/10.1177/13691481221075944.

entries.title: Do populists escalate international disputes?
entries.abstract: Among the potentially most consequential effects of populism is its impact on countries' international conflict behaviour. However, empirical evidence about populists' approach to international disputes is inconclusive. We develop a theoretical framework focused on mobilization and personalization, which we argue are particularly relevant characteristics of populist foreign policy-making. We hypothesize that, on a conflict–cooperation continuum, a country's approach to a bilateral dispute will become more conflictive under a populist government if that dispute is strongly used for domestic political mobilization, and if decision-making on that issue is highly personalized. Conversely, foreign policy will not become more conflictive in cases of weak mobilization and personalization. We carry out in-depth qualitative within-case comparisons of non-populist and populist governments' policies in Bolivia (2002–2019), India (2004–2022), and the Philippines (2010–2022), focusing on two selected bilateral disputes per country. Drawing on a broad range of sources, including 71 expert interviews conducted in the three countries, we find that populists in power escalate international disputes if they strongly use foreign policy issues for domestic mobilization and, at the same time, strongly personalize decision-making. This finding nuances existing assessments about the effect of populism on foreign policy change.
entries.citation: Destradi, Sandra, and Johannes Plagemann. 2024. “Do Populists Escalate International Disputes?” International Affairs 100 (5): 1919–40. https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiae172.

entries.title: Populism: A Very Short Introduction
entries.abstract: What is populism? What is the relationship between populism and democracy? Populism: A Very Short Introduction presents populism as an ideology that divides society into two antagonistic camps: the “pure people” versus the “corrupt elite,” and that privileges popular sovereignty above all else. It illustrates the practical power of this ideology by describing populist movements of the modern era—European right-wing parties, left-wing presidents in Latin America, and the Tea Party movement in the United States—and charismatic populist leaders such as Juan Domingo Péron, H. Ross Perot, Silvio Berlusconi, and Hugo Chávez. Although populism is ultimately part of democracy, populist forces constitute an increasing challenge to democratic politics.
entries.citation: Mudde, Cas, and Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser. 2017. Populism: A Very Short Introduction. 1st ed. Oxford University PressNew York. https://doi.org/10.1093/actrade/9780190234874.001.0001.
